prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at magic twist angles in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, opening the field of moire quantum materials.

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene offers the cleanest theory-to-experiment chain on the shortlist. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted a flat-band condition at a specific twist angle, and the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity by Jarillo-Herrero's group confirmed that a single geometric tuning parameter can drive a clean two-dimensional material into strongly correlated states. The discovery is easy to state, falsifiable, reproduced by many independent groups and techniques, and has generated a large, productive field. It also puts an interacting many-body problem on a highly controllable platform, which is the kind of conceptual bridge between statistical-mechanics ideas and experiment that I value. The credited trio maps naturally onto a prediction and a decisive demonstration, and three of eight members placed it first, so my second place in the opening ballot moves to first after hearing the arguments.
statement.case_against: The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity and the nature of several correlated phases are still debated, so one can argue that the understanding is not yet settled and that eight years is early. The credit is also open: the Cao et al. experimental paper was a group effort, Dean, Young, Yacoby and others made essential related discoveries, and earlier continuum-moire theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto predates Bistritzer-MacDonald in part. A three-name prize necessarily leaves some of these out, and that asymmetry would be criticised.

responses.point: Argues that B009 is an unusually clean theory-to-experiment chain, with the Bistritzer-MacDonald angle predicted from electronic-structure reasoning and then confirmed in 2018, while acknowledging that Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto raise priority questions.
responses.response: I agree on the strength of the chain, and I think it is the main reason to prefer B009 over fields where theory and experiment developed in parallel. I would qualify the priority point more firmly than the opening ballot did: the earlier continuum models identified a reduced Fermi velocity at small angles, whereas the flat-band condition at a definite magic angle, with its quantitative prediction, is the Bistritzer-MacDonald result, and that is what the experiment tested. I still regard the earlier theory as a real attribution risk that the citation wording must handle carefully.

responses.point: Ranks B009 third, accepting the originality and the mechanism but worrying that the origin of superconductivity and the correlated phases is still debated, which makes timing arguable.
responses.response: I share the concern but weigh it differently. The Nobel standard is a robust discovery, not a complete explanation, and the correlated insulators and superconducting domes are reproduced across several moire platforms. Unsettled pairing is common in prizewinning condensed-matter discoveries, and I would phrase the citation around the prediction and the observation of the states, not around their mechanism. I do accept that if the committee wants a stricter maturity bar, B049 is the safer fallback.

responses.point: Puts the optical lattice clocks first as an original, clean, thoroughly confirmed and timely metrology achievement, while treating B009 as strongly confirmed in its facts but possibly early because interpretation is still evolving.
responses.response: I take the maturity argument for B049 seriously and I rate Katori and Ye highly; it is a natural two-person prize with 20 years of independent confirmation. My disagreement is about the scientific weight: the clocks are a refinement of precision measurement, with a close precedent in the 2005 and 2012 prizes, whereas twisted bilayer graphene opened a new class of quantum matter. I would not call B009 premature, but I would not object strongly to B049 if the committee prefers maturity, which is why I list it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Ranks Kane, Mele and Molenkamp first for topological insulators and the Higgs second, on the grounds of maturity and a decisive theory-plus-experiment structure, while noting that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D topological-insulator contributors complicate credit.
responses.response: B026 is mature and conceptually important, and I agree that a theory-plus-experiment trio is natural. But I think its credit problem is more serious than that of B009: the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang was the direct trigger for Molenkamp's experiment, Zhang cannot be recognised, and the 3D work by Fu, Kane, Moore, Hasan and others is a separate chapter. Under a three-person cap that leaves a visible gap in a way that the MacDonald-Bistritzer-Jarillo-Herrero chain does not. On the Higgs, I agree with the point about thousands of collaborators and see no clean way to credit it within the statutes.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would accept that the superconductivity and correlated phases are understood well enough, or would prefer to wait.
How to treat the experimental credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero (Cao, Dean, Young, Yacoby) and the earlier continuum theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) within a three-person limit.

Whether my own first-ranked B011 (active matter) has enough support outside my own field to be a serious contender; only my ballot placed it in the top eight, so I treat it as an alternative, not the lead.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of my documented co-authors or institutional affiliations (Gothenburg, Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg) is among the credited names of the shortlisted candidates. My field of statistical physics of active and complex systems is close to B011, so I note that for transparency.
